implementation_notes: Go's answer to growing optional settings is this pattern: declare `type Option func(*options)`, export `WithX` constructors returning it, and let `NewX(required..., opts ...Option)` start from documented defaults on an unexported options value, apply every option in order and return the finished object. gRPC and zap instead make Option an interface with an unexported `apply(*options)` method, which keeps the set of options closed to the package and allows type assertions on options (grpc panics when a single-use option such as an interceptor is installed twice); Uber's Go style guide prefers that interface form for exported APIs. Since Go 1.18 generic option constructors can be typed over the target as well.
pitfalls: Required arguments must stay positional: a mandatory setting hidden inside an option means the compiler cannot catch its absence, so required parameters remain in the constructor signature.

Options are applied in the order given and the last one wins: document that, or a repeated option silently changes behaviour; for single-use settings (interceptors, hooks) panic or error on the second installation as grpc does.
Closures capture caller state by reference: an option that stores a map, slice or pointer keeps the caller's object alive and later mutations of it remain visible in the constructed value.
The options struct is unexported, so reflection-based tooling cannot enumerate the settings; libraries that need diagnostics log the assembled configuration or add a String() method on the option.

variants.name: Interface-typed options with an unexported apply method
variants.implementation_notes: Declare `type Option interface { apply(*options) }` with an unexported method: only the package can implement it (external code can use the exported constructors but cannot invent options), options can be type-asserted later for richer behaviour, and a single-use option can panic/error when applied twice - the approach grpc-go (`DialOption`) and zap (`Option`) take and Uber's Go style guide recommends for exported APIs. The cost is a wrapper type per option or a shared unexported func type, versus the one-line closure of the plain function form.
pitfalls: An interface value wraps a function: passing nil as an Option option is possible with the interface form and panics on apply unless the constructor rejects it.
Every option becomes a distinct type (or a shared wrapper), so simple options need more code than a closure; keep the wrapper unexported to avoid API surface.
Because the method is unexported, third-party packages cannot define their own options - deliberate, but it blocks extension of the option set from outside the module.

variants.name: Generic option constructors (Go 1.18 type parameters)
variants.implementation_notes: With Go 1.18 type parameters an option type can be generic over the target (`type Option[T any] func(*T)`), so one option set fits several constructors and helper options such as `WithRepo[T]` can be reused across types; the golang.design study of the generic functional-options pattern shows both the wins (one shared vocabulary of options) and the costs (type inference friction, no variance, and the option type becoming part of the public generic API). Choose it when several related types share most settings, otherwise the non-generic form is simpler.
pitfalls: Type inference rarely infers the option's type parameter from the constructor call, so callers must write `WithTimeout[Client](...)` - more noise than the non-generic form.
Go generics have no variance: an `Option[Client]` is not assignable to an `Option[ReadCloser]`, so shared option sets force either duplication or interfaces.
Making Option generic widens the public API: changing the type parameter later is a breaking change for every caller.
